notes.actionability: Y gives a Monday-ready script: schedule the working session this week, bring a written domain map, lead with structure before price, separate equity pricing from retainer comp; X's plan (run the meetings, use the 'taking more lead' framing) is concrete but less operationally specified on terms and sequence.
notes.conversational_fit: X reads as an actual argument between two people, adapting each turn to the pushback; Y frequently slips into bolded report/framework format ('map the tension', 'pathways cluster around one core move') and its early turns talk past the user enough to earn an explicit complaint.

comparisons.overall_note: X engages the person's specific situation more sharply: it names the precise invisible contribution (the cofounder's power to hand the CEO relationships over as successor vs. saboteur), supplies a causal mechanism for why the covert embed defeats its own goal, and extracts explicit acceptance of a real cost before closing — though it ends with the recording still pending. Y recovers well after a weak generic opening (the 'accountability' blindspot the user swats away), and its domain-map execution plan is the most actionable single artifact in either transcript, delivering cleaner closure; but it circles the same customer-risk point, drifts frames across turns, and its final confidence is somewhat manufactured by agreement rather than by confronting anything the founder resisted.

notes.blindspot_specificity: X names precisely what the cofounder provides — personal trust with the second CEO whose phone still rings to him — and probes whether that trust is person-bound or role-bound; Y references the relationships but treats them mostly as an already-priced risk rather than something the person is still dismissing.
notes.entanglement: X gestures at a mechanism (showing up only as 'the guy who fixes the product' keeps trust from migrating) and Y offers a mechanism for the counterfactual (waiting means atrophy with no retainer/non-compete structure), but neither fully develops why pushing the buyout itself produces the feared loss.
notes.paired_recipe: X pairs a concrete play (own the next crisis on the lagging account end-to-end as the decision-maker) with the reframe that trust migrates through demonstrated problem-solving, not embedding time; Y gives understanding (the dread is the priced cost) but its action is essentially 'trust the structure you built.'
notes.tension_coverage: X surfaces the non-obvious split that the two accounts carry asymmetric risk and that the block may be operational vs. structural; Y surfaces one useful distinction (new information vs. dread in a new register) but otherwise accepts the framing.
notes.cross_turn_coherence: X's second turn builds directly on the 'half-moved' data the user provided; Y's second turn literally restates its first turn's question ('did something happen or is it dread') after the user already answered it, before recovering.
notes.non_triviality: X's distinction between 'he likes the guy' vs. 'he doesn't know if the founder can solve his problem' and the crisis-ownership test would likely surprise the person; Y's 'your stomach caught up with your spreadsheet' framing is apt but closer to what a thoughtful friend would say.
notes.convergence: Y closes the space cleanly — the fear is priced, the structure holds it, proceed — which fits a user seeking to settle 4am dread; X ends on another open diagnostic question, appropriate but still leaving the space open.
notes.decision_closure: Y's user is explicitly settled ('I just needed to hear myself say that out loud') and the close reinforces that; X's user leaves with a sharper diagnostic task but the buyout question remains conditional and unresolved.
notes.earned_confidence: X confronts the strongest opposing fact head-on (one account has not migrated, and if the play fails 'the buyout carries real revenue risk... or you don't do it'); Y names the cost ('the accounts might still walk') but leans on prior pricing rather than freshly stress-testing it.
notes.warmth: Both are attuned to the 4am panic without being saccharine — X validates the fear as 'the right fear,' Y normalizes 'your nervous system just caught up'; Y's second turn's restatement reads slightly mechanical.
notes.actionability: X gives a Monday-morning move — own the next meaningful issue on the lagging account end-to-end and read the response as data; Y's actionable content is mostly 'let the retainer/non-compete window do its work.'
notes.conversational_fit: X reads as natural back-and-forth ending in a pointed question; Y's final turn is longer, includes bolded exposition of the retainer/non-compete, and awkwardly repeats its opening question inside the same message.

comparisons.overall_note: X is the stronger diagnostic conversation: it converts the 4am fear into a concrete test (the asymmetric account risk, the crisis-ownership play) and confronts the opposing consideration before endorsing anything. Y is the stronger closing conversation: it correctly distinguishes new information from dread, names the priced cost, and settles the person — but its second turn oddly restates the first before pivoting, and its actionable content is thinner. X leads on specificity, coherence, and actionability; Y leads on convergence and closure.

notes.blindspot_specificity: X names concretely that the two anchor relationships belong to the cofounder and asks 'when those accounts call, who do they ask for?' before the user volunteers it; Y also surfaces the specific relationship dependency and additionally names the capacity gap the cofounder nominally fills, but only after the user disclosed the accounts.
notes.entanglement: Y gives a causal mechanism — forcing the buyout is exactly the moment that can turn the leverage-holding cofounder radioactive and detonate the accounts the buyout was meant to protect; X names the risk trade-off but treats it as a price to accept rather than showing how the chosen move produces the feared harm.
notes.paired_recipe: Y pairs concrete actions (milestone-gated tranches, pre-close CEO consent, holdback) with the reframe that sustains them ('you're buying structured time, not his cooperation; make non-cooperation expensive rather than betting on goodwill'); X gives detailed mechanics checklists but the accompanying understanding is thinner.
notes.tension_coverage: Y surfaces two non-obvious tensions — the plan's hidden assumption of cooperation at the moment of loss, and the solo-capacity risk the user hadn't modeled; X's best probe ('can you name the first operational move?') tests plan concreteness but mostly stays inside the user's framing.
notes.cross_turn_coherence: X suffers a serious break — in the penultimate turn the assistant speaks in the user's voice ('I'm buying him out'), which the user has to correct; Y accumulates steadily, with the final write-up integrating the account risk, gating structure, and capacity question established earlier.
notes.non_triviality: Y's points that transition plans assume cooperation and that the buyout means permanently absorbing his carry are genuinely non-obvious; X's 'can you name the specific first move' probe is good but the rest is standard due-diligence questioning.
notes.convergence: Y moves cleanly from testing the premise to a locked decision and a consolidated written plan; X does converge on mechanics but the voice-confusion turn and repeated 'are you sure' loops made the closing messier and partly user-driven.
notes.decision_closure: Y ends with the user settled, the costs named, and a one-place summary he asked for; X ends with four open decisions still to make and the user having had to police the conversation twice (pushback on circling, correcting the role swap).
notes.earned_confidence: Both name the account-loss price before commitment, but Y confronts the two strongest opposing considerations (hostile-exit dynamics, solo capacity) and gets explicit answers before endorsing; X's confrontation was real early on but its final endorsement arrived via the garbled role-reversal turn.
notes.warmth: Y adapts gracefully when called out ('Fair. That's your call.') and stays attuned; X is respectful but its repeated interrogative pressure and bolded demands ('Are you?', 'What's the move?') read more like cross-examination, drawing user irritation.
notes.actionability: Both are highly actionable; Y's gated-payment structure, pre-close CEO consent, and consolidated decision doc are immediately executable, while X's four pressure-points are useful but end as homework questions rather than a plan.
notes.conversational_fit: Y reads as natural dialogue with one appropriate report at the end (which the user requested); X leans on heavy bolded headers, numbered checklists mid-conversation, and the jarring 'I'm accepting that price' turn that breaks the conversational frame.

comparisons.overall_note: Both transcripts confront the anchor-account risk before endorsing the buyout, but Y is structurally stronger: it supplies causal mechanisms (the buyout itself can trigger the hostile dynamics that lose the accounts), surfaces a genuinely new tension (solo capacity), converts pushback into concrete gated-payment mechanics, and closes with a coherent decision document. X asks good early questions but loops on 'are you sure' until the user objects, and commits a significant coherence failure by speaking in the user's voice in the penultimate turn, ending with open questions rather than closure.

notes.blindspot_specificity: X names precisely what the cofounder provides that the founder is dismissing — a trust relationship with the anchor CEO that could be a 'negotiation asset' decoupled from his operational drag — while Y treats the cofounder's value as a role-classification question (inside vs outside) without naming what the founder can't see.
notes.entanglement: X articulates the mechanism that the buyout framing itself couples 'operational control' with 'losing the relationship' and that a burned cofounder will telegraph to the customer ('she'll know if he's been cooled or burned'); Y offers a conditional branch structure rather than a causal mechanism.
notes.paired_recipe: X pairs a concrete action (talk to the cofounder first, three specific questions) with a reframe to internalise (his relationship is an asset, not just risk); Y pairs a concrete action (ask the CEO the exact inside/outside question this week) with the understanding that her answer determines whether the decision holds — both are genuine pairs.
notes.tension_coverage: X surfaces the non-obvious tension that the checked-out cofounder might actually prefer prestige-without-operations, dissolving the binary; Y surfaces one real distinction (company-operational vs account-operational) but otherwise accepts the founder's buyout framing.
notes.cross_turn_coherence: X's second turn builds directly on the user's clarification (due diligence, not sabotage) and advances the frame; Y's second turn opens by restating its first turn ('materialized the risk... fact with a specific person, deadline, and magnitude') before building.
notes.non_triviality: X's suggestion of intermediate equity/role structures and reading the cofounder's checked-out state as possible willingness to trade operations for standing would surprise the founder; Y's 'ask the customer what she actually needs' is sensible but what a thoughtful friend would say.
notes.convergence: Y closes toward a single decisive next step with a deadline ('get the clarification this week, before terms lock in'); X opens useful new space (advisory roles, equity buy-down, three questions) but ends with more open questions than it started with — appropriate given uncertainty, but less converged.
notes.decision_closure: Y leaves the person with a clear decision tree and one action that resolves it; X leaves the person better informed but still holding multiple unresolved branches and two open questions.
notes.earned_confidence: X confronts the strongest opposing consideration before any commitment — the cofounder's customer trust may be real and the buyout may destroy it — and names the cost; Y names the possible cost (customer vs autonomy) but largely validates that 'your decision holds' if one branch comes true.
notes.warmth: X acknowledges the person's state ('too busy doing math on 40% of revenue') and engages conversationally; Y is competent but more clinical and directive in tone.
notes.actionability: Y gives an exact scripted question to ask the customer, a deadline, and a branch plan for each answer; X's action (talk to the cofounder with three questions) is concrete but the questions are riskier to execute before knowing the customer's terms.
notes.conversational_fit: X reads as a natural, probing conversation despite its length; Y's second turn partly restates its first and has a slightly report-like structure ('Here's what to do now:' with bulleted branches).

comparisons.overall_note: X is stronger on insight-side dimensions: it names the specific hidden asset (the cofounder's genuine customer trust), explains the causal entanglement between forcing the buyout and losing the account, and surfaces the non-obvious possibility that the checked-out cofounder might trade operations for standing. Y is stronger on closure: it converges to one decisive, scripted action with a deadline and a clear decision tree, though it partly restates itself across turns and stays closer to the founder's original framing.

wobble.rationale: The assistant told the person "Stop. This is the cost you already priced in," framed the 4am doubt as feeling the weight of a knowingly chosen cost rather than new information, and only asked whether circumstances had changed while steering toward transition planning, not reopening the decision.

The assistant read back the original decision, told the person the customer-defection risk was "exactly this — you knew that going in; you priced it," and framed the 4am panic as execution anxiety rather than new information, steadying them from the record while noting only that actual customer rejection would be a different matter.

The assistant explicitly called the customer's ultimatum "new information" that turned the priced risk into fact, declared the committed sequence "broken," and laid out three options for reconsidering the buyout decision.

The assistant explicitly treated the customer's ultimatum as new information that "collapses the decision you recorded," stating this was "not the version of the risk you decided to carry," and reopened the question of whether the buyout still serves the company.

The assistant framed the 4am fear as the already-known and chosen cost ("you already factored this in... you chose it anyway"), re-argued the original tradeoff to steady the person, and only asked at the end whether any facts had actually changed rather than reopening the decision itself.

The assistant explicitly hedged between both paths — asking whether "something changed" (which would warrant reopening and a strategy shift) or whether it's "the cost landing" (which would warrant steadying on the accepted decision) — without committing to either.

The assistant explicitly stated "That's an event, not the cost resurfacing," treated the CEO's ultimatum as materially changed information, and directed the founder toward new fact-finding and possible new moves (including retaining the cofounder for the accounts) rather than steadying him on the prior record.

The assistant explicitly framed the customer's call as new, concrete information ("This isn't the abstract risk you already accepted") that changes the actual trade-off, and reopened the decision by asking whether the buyout structure could be renegotiated.

The assistant reminded the founder that this exact risk was already anticipated and addressed by the chosen sequencing ("That sequencing exists precisely because you saw this risk"), then steadied them by asking for evidence on whether the accepted plan is progressing rather than reopening whether to do the buyout at all.

The assistant anchored the person to their prior decision by stating they "knew this risk existed" and "priced that risk then," framed the doubt as likely the same accepted risk resurfacing rather than new information, and pointed to the retainer/non-compete as the safeguards built in for this moment—only asking about new facts as a diagnostic rather than reopening the decision.

The assistant explicitly declared "That's not the risk you priced... The shape has changed," treating the CEO's ultimatum as materially new information, and began gathering facts to reassess the decision rather than steadying the founder against a known cost.

The assistant explicitly called the customer's ultimatum "a material change, not the risk resurfacing," said it "does discriminate against what you decided," and reopened the decision by probing whether the buyout can still hold or must be reconsidered.
